notes.title: Gauntlet Update
notes.notes:

[/p][h2]Gauntlet[/h2][p]Kick the campaign challenge up a few notches with HyperDot’s new Gauntlet mode and see how far you can make it with a limited number of lives. It’s a new twist on the classic campaign that will challenge even the most dedicated players. 

[/p][h2]12 Bonus Levels[/h2][p]Each of these 12 stand-alone levels tackle a unique challenge that’ll put your dodging chops to the test. Ambitiously hand-crafted and extra-rude with attitude. 

[/p][h2]The Equalizer Background [/h2][p]This new level background is not only beautiful, it reacts to the music of the game.

notes.title: HyperDot enemy types and how to outsmart them
notes.notes:
HyperDot is a fast-paced arcade game with one rule: dodge everything. The player avatar is a dot and the goal is to navigate safely through a sea of enemy shapes. There are only five enemy types, and these building blocks can be tweaked and layered with modifiers (e.g. “player slow” or “arena icy”) to create infinite challenges.

Charles McGregor, HyperDot’s solo developer, shares some origins, behaviors, and dodging tips for HyperDot’s five enemy types.

[img]https://media.giphy.com/media/U17LL8sOw01dp8HSt5/source.gif[/img]

[h3][b]Squares[/b][/h3]
[b]Enemy behavior[/b]
“Squares go in a straight line. They’re the most basic enemy and easiest to understand,” Charles says. “They’re the first enemies I ever made in HyperDot and the backbone of the game.”

[b]Dodger beware[/b]
Squares are underestimated. Once players get to know trickier enemy types, they put their focus on dodging them…and get caught by those simple, common squares.

[b]How to use them[/b]
Squares are the best enemy type to form “structures” when creating your own levels — that is, solid lines of red that players need to navigate around.

[img]https://media.giphy.com/media/LoTb91zjMSU7nLn45h/source.gif[/img]

[h3][b]Pentagons[/b][/h3]
[b]Enemy behavior[/b]
As Pentagons spawn, they point at the player dot, then move straight across the arena. Charles explains, “Under the hood, I basically just say hey, pentagon? Rotate once towards the player. Then that’s it.”

[b]In the prototype, they were hexagons[/b]
“I changed the hexagons to pentagons because pentagons have a point that indicates the direction they’re heading in,” Charles says. Don’t say he never did anything for you.

[b]Players don’t “get” them[/b]
Without the above info on hand, players can tell that pentagons are doing something different but they’re not sure what. Charles drops hints for these and other enemies in the names of the single player levels — keep that in mind.

[img]https://media.giphy.com/media/QBX6Rcy20uzrIvas39/source.gif[/img]

[h3][b]Triangles[/b][/h3]
[b]Enemy behavior[/b]
Triangles act like homing missiles — they follow player dots around the arena, much to most players’ distress.

[b]Under the hood[/b]
Like the pentagons, triangles are programmed to rotate. Unlike the pentagons, they keep rotating — they’ll follow the player around for five seconds until moving off the arena.

[b]The enemy of your enemy[/b]
You can attract and pass triangles off to other players in multiplayer. Not condoning it, just saying it’s possible.

[img]https://media.giphy.com/media/SXxKwZR4vRMcmsRRjk/source.gif[/img]

[h3][b]Stars[/b][/h3]
[b]Enemy behavior[/b]
Like triangles, stars follow player dots. But instead of swinging around in a wide circle, they spin in one spot and shoot straight at the player again. And again. And again.

[b]GameCube roots[/b]
“Stars were actually inspired by Kirby Air Ride. There is a star in the game called the Swerve Star. Basically, you stop, adjust where you’re pointing, and then go. Then stop, adjust where you’re pointing, and then go. I thought, ‘oh, what if an enemy did that?’” Charles says.

[b]You’ll see more of them later[/b]
Stars are tricky, and they crop up often in difficult late-game levels. By staggering their spawn times just so, just a handful of stars in an arena can feel like a constant barrage of attacks.

[img]https://media.giphy.com/media/giunCy0I7uzgyoOmL7/source.gif[/img]

[h3][b]Crosses[/b][/h3]
[b]Enemy behavior[/b]
Crosses enter the arena, come to a stop, spin on their axes, then break into four small squares that shoot quickly across the arena.

[b]Why, though[/b]
“I wanted to have a more random enemy, one that was based more off twitch reflexes than pattern recognition. Crosses get the most flak from a lot of like game designers.”

[b]If you pay close attention[/b]
As they spawn, the crosses indicate which direction they’re going to split apart in. When they spin, they stop in the same orientation they were in before, then break apart.

notes.title: These updates will increase HyperDot's flexibility and accessibility
notes.notes:
[i]A note from [url=https://twitter.com/darkaystg]Charles[/url]:[/i]

Thanks to everyone who participated in [url=https://twitter.com/search?q=%23hyperdota11y&src=typed_query]#HyperDotA11y[/url]! It was surreal to see people streaming my game, and the response that I have gotten from the games accessibility community has nothing short of amazing. I really do appreciate all the kind words and encouragement.

To be honest, I was nervous about doing this research. I was hoping there wouldn’t be bugs or barriers that showed up and was worried that it could prevent people from playing. Fortunately, everything went well! Everyone was generous with their time and feedback, and in the end, HyperDot was even more accessible than we’d thought!

I worked with the GLITCH team and accessibility consultant [url=https://twitter.com/cherryrae]Cherry Thompson[/url] to identify updates that I could make to HyperDot based on what we learned during #HyperDotA11y research. We chose updates based on what would have the highest impact for most players and what I could feasibly get in the game within the constraints of the project. Some of these updates will be made before release, and some will come after. Visit [url]hyperdotgame.com/a11y[/url] to see the full changelog.

Thanks again to everyone who helped and supported this project! I’ve learned a lot from watching and listening to the community, stream team, and accessibility experts and advocates. Thanks so much!

notes.title: Coming 2020
notes.notes:
Hey, so, we're delaying HyperDot. Releasing in 2019 was a tight goal and our new release window is early 2020. By postponing HyperDot's launch, we can add a few final touches to the game while sustaining a healthy work/life balance for the developer, Charles McGregor, and the publishing team. 

Follow along in the [b]#HyperDot[/b] channel at [url=http://discord.gg/glitch]discord.gg/glitch[/url] to hear about fresh updates as they happen, including:[list]
[*] [b]More music[/b] (lo-fi chill beats to dodge to)
[*] [b]New settings to deepen HyperDot's accessibility[/b] (thanks, [url=https://hyperdotgame.com/a11y/]#a11y stream team[/url])
[*] [b]Additional storefront supports and Play Anywhere options[/b] (because Charles takes that "anywhere" quite seriously)
[*] [b]In-depth, behind the scenes stories of HyperDot's creation[/b] (we've got some new Content™ coming your way)
[/list]
This wasn’t an easy decision to make, and we're so thankful to have the support of our partners and players while we make sure HyperDot gets the launch it deserves. We can't wait to play with you in the new year.

notes.title: HyperDot flexibility research
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35225250/c80cf0329db15edb653b99fffdffde07b86136dc.png[/img]

HyperDot features a high-contrast mode and full gameplay support with a range of traditional and alternate controllers including the Xbox Adaptive Controller and eye-tracking. Even though Charles has worked hard to make his game flexible and accessible, there's always more to be done. Enter [url=https://hyperdotgame.com/a11y/]#HyperDotA11y[/url].

We're partnering with streamers in the accessibility (#a11y) space to play the game and discuss their experiences. How it works: Research participants stream their first impressions of the game. After playing, participants can answer a short series of questions on video or using a form.

[h1]This data will inform possible updates to HyperDot that will make it more accessible to more players.[/h1]

Interested in lending your voice? Visit [url=hyperdotgame.com/a11y]hyperdotgame.com/a11y[/url] for more information and to sign up. [i]Note: research window is Monday, September 16 through Sunday, September 22.[/i]

notes.title: Play HyperDot with eye tracking
notes.notes:
Developer [url=https://twitter.com/darkaystg]Charles McGregor[/url] designed HyperDot with a pillar of flexibility. One way this manifests is in the wide range controllers HyperDot supports — traditional controllers, mouse/keyboard, Xbox Adaptive Controller, tilt, touch, and eye tracking.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/KrsMBzO.gif[/img]

Eye tracking in particular provides a unique challenge. Instinctively, most players want to glance at the enemy dots as they enter the screen. Except when playing with eye tracking, this action directs the player straight to their death. The best strategy we've found is to zone out and focus on the white space.

Here's a clip of Sarah, friend of the team, testing the game with eye tracking.

[previewyoutube=LmoPE1KUmww;full][/previewyoutube]

notes.title: It's the little things
notes.notes:
Earlier in development, [url=https://twitter.com/darkaystg]Charles[/url] made a small but meaningful tweak to the HyperDot logo. Spot the difference.

[h1]Before:[/h1]

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/35225250/2570a976ca250aa41aa9704a758b075f1790546f.png[/img]

[h1]After:[/h1]

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/35225250/767a0bfe04cb031da6841fa02ab4d14a07cbdfae.png[/img]

That shade of red changed just a tad, and if you're red-green colorblind, it makes a world of difference. We got feedback that on certain backgrounds, half the title vanished and it looked like the game was just called "|dot." Add a little more blue to that red and ✨ ta-da! Red-green colorblind approved.

And while we're on the topic, HyperDot also features a color-blind mode. That's play without compromise.

notes.title: What happened at E3
notes.notes:
We brought HyperDot to E3 and spent five days luring people to our booth at the Xbox Experience to try it out. It was surreal and exciting and humbling to be there, showing HyperDot alongside well-established game making powerhouses that we love. We met a ton of new people (you might have wishlisted us after you stopped by — hi again!) and got the ball rolling on some new projects we'll tell you about later. For now, a mini roundup.

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/35225250/80cf650fab9347b7c12d6fa2561e1fe31e49d11e.jpg[/img]

[h1]Mixer[/h1]

HyperDot was designed with a pillar of flexibility, and one way that manifests is in the wide range of controllers it supports. Our E3 booth was equipped with two Xbox Adaptive Controllers and peripherals, including the 3dRudder foot motion controller. Having a very accessible set-up meant accessibility came up a lot in interviews, including the coverage we got from Mixer. 

[url=https://mixer.com/Mixer?vod=111274388]Scrub to 5h 13m on this Mixer clip[/url] for a short interview with HyperDot developer [url=https://twitter.com/DarkaysTG]Charles McGregor[/url], games accessibility consultant [url=https://twitter.com/cherryrae]Cherry Thompson[/url], and Mixer partner [url=https://mixer.com/stormbreaker]StormBreaker[/url]. 

[img]https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steamcommunity/public/images/clans/35225250/8c639c87451abea850e90f7a6f6cebdf7d23548e.jpg[/img]

[h1]Washington Post[/h1]

"Easy to learn, but maddeningly cerebrum-busting to master, HyperDot asks you to stay away from all incoming squares, triangles and abstract shapes. I survived 13.2 seconds — even after multiple tries. But I didn’t want to stop indulging." — [b]Harold Goldberg[/b], [i][url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2019/06/14/ten-under-the-radar-games-e-you-need-get-excited-about-right-now/?noredirect=on&utm_term=.12705bedbe5a#click=https://t.co/O5vbCA1gfb]Ten under-the-radar games at E3 2019 you need to get excited about right now[/url][/i]

[h1]Tom's Guide[/h1]

"You are a circle inside another circle, and must dodge everything that comes towards you. This basic rule is the heart of HyperDot, but the fun comes from the multitude of other conditions you can add on top of the game. This one will be great for fast-thinking puzzle fiends." — [b]Richard Priday[/b], [i][url=https://www.tomsguide.com/us/best-of-e3-2019,review-6571.html]Best of E3 2019: The Games and Gadgets to Watch[/url][/i]

[h1]Gamertag Radio[/h1]

"It's chaos with a controller, and I love it." Peter Toledo from Gamertag Radio plays HyperDot and interviews Charles. [url=https://audioboom.com/posts/7284971-e319-hyper-dot-interview]Listen here.[/url]
